parts: Light is the form of energy that makes things visible. Objects that give out their own light (sun, candle, firefly) are luminous; others (moon, a steel plate) are seen by the light they reflect. Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a surface; a smooth, shiny surface that reflects most light is a mirror. Laws of reflection: (1) the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane; (2) the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r). Speed, frequency and wavelength do not change on reflection. A smooth surface gives regular reflection; a rough surface scatters light in all directions (diffused reflection), though each ray still obeys the laws.

A real image is formed where reflected (or refracted) rays actually meet; it can be taken on a screen. A virtual image is formed where rays only appear to meet; it cannot be taken on a screen. A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted (left appears right). If the object moves towards the mirror at v, the image moves towards the object at 2v. A mirror half your height is enough to see your full image.

A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere: in a concave mirror the reflecting surface curves inward; in a convex mirror it bulges outward. Terms: pole (P) — centre of the mirror; centre of curvature (C); radius of curvature (R) = PC; principal axis — line through P and C; principal focus (F) — where rays parallel to the axis meet after reflection (concave) or appear to come from (convex); focal length f = PF, with R = 2f. Rays used in diagrams: a ray parallel to the axis passes through (or appears to come from) F; a ray through F becomes parallel; a ray through C returns along its path; a ray to the pole reflects at an equal angle.

Concave mirror: object at infinity — image at F, real, inverted, highly diminished; beyond C — between F and C, real, inverted, diminished; at C — at C, real, inverted, same size; between C and F — beyond C, real, inverted, enlarged; at F — at infinity, highly enlarged; between F and P — behind the mirror, virtual, erect, enlarged. Convex mirror: for any position the image is behind the mirror between P and F, virtual, erect and diminished.

Uses: plane mirrors in looking glasses, periscopes and kaleidoscopes; concave mirrors in torches, searchlights and vehicle headlights, solar cookers, shaving and dentists' mirrors, reflecting telescopes; convex mirrors as rear-view mirrors in vehicles and at dangerous corners, because they always give an erect, smaller image of a wide field of view.

Sign convention: all distances are measured from the pole; distances in the direction of incident light are positive and opposite to it negative; heights above the axis are positive. Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. Magnification m = height of image / height of object (= −v/u for a mirror).

Refraction is the bending of light when it passes obliquely from one medium to another, because its speed changes. Going from a rarer to a denser medium (air to glass) light slows down and bends towards the normal; from denser to rarer it speeds up and bends away from the normal. A ray falling along the normal goes straight. A coin in water looks raised for this reason. Frequency (and colour) do not change; speed and wavelength do. Laws: (1) the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane; (2) Snell's law — sin i / sin r is a constant, the refractive index n. Also n = speed of light in vacuum / speed of light in the medium; light is slowest in the medium with the largest n. A diamond sparkles because of its very high refractive index.

A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one curved. A convex (converging) lens is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays to a focus; a concave (diverging) lens is thinner in the middle and spreads them out as if from a focus. Rays used: a ray parallel to the axis passes through (or appears to come from) the focus; a ray through the optical centre goes straight.

Convex lens: object at infinity — image at F, real, inverted, highly diminished; beyond 2F — between F and 2F, real, inverted, diminished; at 2F — at 2F, real, inverted, same size; between F and 2F — beyond 2F, real, inverted, enlarged; at F — at infinity; between F and the optical centre — on the same side, virtual, erect, enlarged (a magnifying glass). Concave lens: always a virtual, erect, diminished image between F and the lens.

Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u (f positive for a convex lens, negative for a concave lens). Magnification m = h′/h = v/u. Power of a lens P = 1/f (f in metres); its unit is the dioptre (D). A convex lens has positive power, a concave lens negative. Example: an object 20 cm from a convex lens of focal length 15 cm gives an image 60 cm on the other side, real, inverted and three times as large. A lens of focal length 10 cm gives an image of the same size when the object is at 2F, i.e. 20 cm away.

When white light passes through a glass prism it splits into seven colours — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red (VIBGYOR); this is dispersion. It happens because the refractive index of glass is different for different colours, so they bend by different amounts: violet bends the most and red the least. The band of colours is a spectrum. A rainbow is formed by dispersion of sunlight by raindrops. Visible light has wavelengths about 400–700 nm; longer than red is infrared and shorter than violet is ultraviolet.

The eye lens forms a real, inverted, diminished image on the retina; the ciliary muscles change its focal length so that both near and far objects are seen clearly — the power of accommodation. A normal eye sees from infinity (far point) to 25 cm (near point, the least distance of distinct vision). The visual angle is the angle an object makes at the eye; distant objects look small because their visual angle is small. The eye is relaxed when looking at far objects.

Myopia (short-sightedness): distant objects are not clear because the image forms in front of the retina; corrected with a concave (diverging) lens of negative power. Hypermetropia (long-sightedness): near objects are not clear because the image forms behind the retina; corrected with a convex (converging) lens of positive power. Presbyopia: in old age the muscles weaken and both near and far vision suffer; corrected with bifocal lenses. Astigmatism: the eye lens is not perfectly spherical, so lines in different directions are not seen clearly together; corrected with cylindrical lenses. A person using a +2 D lens is long-sighted; one using a −2 D lens is short-sighted.
